To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the DRL algorithms do not learn to map or to plan, but, rather, they learn to navigate.
DRL-based navigation is not a form of path-planning or mapping.
(i) DRL algorithms do not learn to map or to plan paths, and (ii) they do not learn to navigate in a way that can replace classical algorithms for mapping and path planning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether DRL algorithms are able to learn to navigate in mazes.
the question of whether DRL algorithms are doing some form of path-planning and/or mapping.
the following question: what are DRL algorithms actually doing in the maze navigation task?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the current form, the DRL-based algorithms cannot be considered as “learning to navigate”.
DRL-based navigation algorithms are not able to map and do not learn to navigate in the sense that they do not plan paths to the goal.
, at least with the current DRL-based algorithms, one should not expect that they are learning any mapping or path-plannning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DRL-based navigation algorithms do not do mapping and path planning, but they learn to navigate by using a wall-following behavior.
DRL algorithms do not learn to map and/or navigate in the mazes.
the DRL algorithms are able to learn a strategy that is effective for the given set of mazes but they do not learn a strategy that can be applied to new mazes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DRL algorithms are able to find a goal but they do not learn how to map and plan.
, while the DRL-based algorithms can be used for finding the goal, they cannot be used as mapping or path planning algorithms.
DRL algorithms are not yet ready to replace the mapping and path-planners in the robotics community.
